7.20.1.en: Lest it be understood from his words, "Be not wise overmuch" [16], that we should be slack in seeking wisdom, the Preacher declares his sincere longing for wisdom and his striving to attain it, so that he may be delivered from the folly bound up with evil.

7.20.2.en: "All this have I proved by wisdom:

7.20.3.en: I said, I will be wise;

7.20.4.en: but it was far from me.

7.20.5.en: That which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out?

7.20.6.en: I applied mine heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom, and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness" [23-25].

7.20.7.en: He set all his resolve on attaining wisdom as a way to righteousness; with all his heart, his feelings and his senses he studied, searched, prayed and sought... Thus the heart is joined with the mind, and study with prayer..., working with his whole being and all his abilities to obtain the heavenly wisdom, which is exceedingly far off and exceedingly deep... God gives it to those who seek it.

7.20.8.en: * So also Solomon, who was wiser than all men in his days or in the days before him, to whom God gave largeness of heart and an abundance of contemplation more plentiful than the sand of the sea, yet he too, the deeper he entered into (wisdom), the more his perplexity increased, and he declared his discovery of how very far wisdom is from him.

7.20.9.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * To what extent does man pursue wisdom? And where is its perfection reached?

7.20.10.en: Truly, the limits of this journey cannot be reached, so that even the saints are found lacking in the perfection of wisdom, for there is no end to the journey of wisdom.

7.20.11.en: Wisdom thus rises until it grants the one who follows it union with God. And this is the connection: that the insight of wisdom is without limit, and that wisdom is God Himself.

7.20.12.en: St. Isaac the Syrian As much as the wise Solomon strives in seeking the wisdom that is bound up with righteousness, he also strives to be delivered from the folly bound up with evil, especially from the attachment to wicked women with whom he commits sin... For he found in the adulterous woman the following:

7.21.0.en: a. More bitter than death [26], for she causes the destruction of the soul eternally.

7.21.1.en: b. Deceitful; he calls her "snares," for with sweet and gentle words she sets traps [26].

7.21.2.en: c. Violent; she captures a man as with bonds [26], so that man loses his inner freedom, the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

7.22.0.en: d. Not truthful and not faithful, for the Preacher says: "One man among a thousand have I found; but a woman among all those have I not found" [28]. The wise man discovered that among the crowd that accompanied him, which knew nothing but hypocrisy and flattery along with a life of amusement and luxury, he could scarcely find one man who was frank and sincere in his love among a thousand men, and among the corrupt foreign women he did not find a single one who was truthful.

7.22.1.en: * It is better to renounce that woman and flee from before her, for she is a fowler's snare, and her heart is a trap, and in her hands are bonds. But the one who is righteous before God escapes from her, while the sinner falls into her snares.

7.23.0.en: St. Cyril the Great Lest anyone think that God created man evil, or that woman is more wicked than man, the wise man completed his discourse: "Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" [29]. Man, whether man or woman, has corrupted his life by his many inventions, that is, by his evil conduct and his corrupt will.

7.23.1.en: * He says that He made man upright. Consider the force of these words, for the word man means both male and female... Let us read the beginning of the book of Genesis, and we find "Adam," that is, man, meaning both the man and the woman (for Eve was in Adam), and God created him upright and good; but when we sinned we fell into a wretched state, and left the paradise that had been made good...

7.23.2.en: St. Jerome * The virtue of man and woman is one; as soon as He created them, they were surrounded with equal honor. Hear the book of Genesis: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27). Since their nature is one and they have the same actions, their rewards must also be one.

7.23.3.en: St. Basil the Great * (Speaking in the person of the martyr Julitta)

7.23.4.en: We are of the same clay as men... and like them we were created in the image of God. Yes, woman is able to work virtue as men do. So the Creator willed. And in all things we are nothing but partners with them. God did not take only from the flesh of Adam to make Eve, but she is "bone of his bones" (Gen 2:23). Therefore we owe to the eternal God honor in our steadfastness, in our strength and in our patience, in the same measure as men.

7.23.5.en: St. Basil the Great * The Holy Spirit says: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" [29]. Thus it is evident that men from the beginning discovered evil, wrestled with it and imagined it in themselves, and they deserved the penalty of death with which they had been threatened. And from that time they did not return to what they had been, but were corrupted by their inventions.

7.23.6.en: Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic * We were created good by the Good (God), for "God made man upright," but by our free will we became evil. We had the power to become evil, and we were good, and we shall have the strength to become good while we are evil.

7.23.7.en: * So, as it is written: "God hath made man upright" [29], and therefore with a good will, for if he had not had a good will he would not have been counted upright. Then the good will is of God's making, for God created him with it. But the first evil will, which preceded all the evil works of man, is rather a kind of falling away from the work of God...

7.23.8.en: St. Augustine * The wise Solomon says: "God hath made man upright," that is, to enjoy the knowledge of what is good only, "but they have sought out many imaginations," that they - as it was said - wanted to know good and evil.

7.23.9.en: Abba Chaeremon * Because we sin by our free will, the prophet says plainly in a certain place: Though I planted for you a fruitful vine... how are you turned into bitterness and become a strange vine? The plant was good, but the fruit came from the evil will. Therefore the vinedresser is not blamed, but the vine is burned with fire, because it was planted good but bore the fruits of evil by its own will.

7.23.10.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * We must not ascribe the deviation into the wandering of the heart to human nature or to its Creator. For the Holy Scripture rightly says: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." The difference of thoughts depends on us, for the good thought draws near to those who know it, and the prudent man finds it (Prov 19:7). So whatever is subject to our discernment and our work, we are able to attain; and if we do not reach it, this is due to our laziness and neglect, not to a fault in our nature.

8.0.1.en: and who knoweth the interpretation of a thing?

8.0.2.en: a man's wisdom maketh his face to shine, and the boldness of his face shall be changed" [1].

8.0.3.en: Many are afflicted with a kind of frustration or indifference when they contemplate the vanity of the world and the injustice and oppression that prevail in it, especially on the part of those entrusted with justice, whether on the religious or the civil level. Therefore the Preacher begins to reveal the importance of wisdom in man's life, regardless of what goes on around him.

8.0.4.en: a. Wisdom makes a man advance ahead of his kinsmen and makes him more distinguished than they: "Who is as the wise man?" Heavenly wisdom, as we saw before, is without limit, far off, that is, exalted to the utmost height and exceeding deep (Eccl 7:24); it lifts man up to God to grant him a life of fellowship and union with Him. There is no learned, noble or rich man who can compare with the one who enjoys divine wisdom!

8.0.5.en: When the wise Solomon spoke in the book of Proverbs about wisdom as a living being (Prov 9:1-6), he meant by it the person of the Lord Christ, "the wisdom of the Father." The wise man is the one who receives the Lord Christ dwelling in him, or receives Him as his head, and is himself a member of the Church, the Body of Christ.

8.0.6.en: Our union with the Lord Christ gives the heart sweetness and breadth, and lifts the mind above all troubles and trivialities, so that it walks in the Spirit of Christ with balance and heavenly wisdom.

8.0.7.en: b. Wisdom makes a man useful to his brethren, devoted in his service to them, for one like him "knoweth the interpretation of a thing," that is, he perceives what lies behind events and follows the purposes of things on a higher level... His counsel to them is wise and sound. For wisdom gives him an interpretation of dealings with him as with others, so that he walks and guides others according to God's good will.

8.0.8.en: c. By wisdom man comes to know God's plan and understands why relief is permitted as well as affliction, so his face is enlightened with joy and hope under all circumstances, and he even sends forth this joyful hope into the lives of his friends, so that his image appears beautiful and radiant in their eyes. Thus wisdom makes his face shine, as happened with Moses the prophet when he came down from the mountain. It honors him and lends radiance to all his speech. It makes him worthy of the attention and reverence of others, beloved by them, and changes the hardness of his face, his speech and the sternness of his features into radiant and cheerful features.

8.0.9.en: d. Wisdom (the Lord Christ) reforms the violent nature of man, for "the boldness of his face shall be changed"... It gives him enlightenment and tenderness!

8.0.10.en: * The nearer man's heart draws to wisdom, the greater the joy it receives from God. By this a person can distinguish between spiritual wisdom and worldly wisdom. And man is assured in himself that spiritual wisdom causes a silence that settles in his depths, while worldly wisdom causes a flood of slipping into error.

8.0.11.en: When you discover spiritual wisdom, you are filled with humility, gentleness and a peace that rules over our thoughts, so your members are calm and wicked passions and gluttony do not disturb you. But if the other wisdom takes possession of you, then a haughty mind takes hold of you, together with perverse and unspeakable thoughts, a scattered mind and shameful, inflamed senses!

8.0.12.en: * How sweet is the knowledge that is acquired from real experience and diligent exercises. And how great is the power it gives to the man who finds it within himself through many experiences; the same is felt by those who are certain of it and remember how much help it has provided them, so they know the weakness of their nature and perceive the measure of the divine help granted to them, which God may withhold at the beginning while they are in the midst of trials.

8.0.13.en: * The knowledge that concerns God is the queen of all longings; there is nothing sweeter than it on all the earth for the heart that receives it.

8.0.14.en: * When does a man perceive that he has received wisdom from the Spirit? From the knowledge that teaches him the ways of humility in his hidden depths and in his senses, and reveals to him in his mind how humility is obtained.

8.0.15.en: St. Isaac the Syrian St. John Chrysostom compares the beauty that wisdom reflects on a woman's features with the care for outward adornment, saying: [If a man's wisdom makes his face to shine, how much more will a woman's virtue make her countenance shine? And if you count this a great adornment, tell me what will be the value of pearls on that (last) day?].

8.1.0.en: 2 I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God. 3 Be not hasty to go out of his sight: stand not in an evil thing; for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him. 4 Where the word of a king is, there is power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou? 5 Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment.

8.1.1.en: Since wisdom is a meeting with God Himself, the true "Wisdom," the face of the believer is enlightened and carries within it a surpassing sweetness with a spirit of humility... this inner humility must be translated in practice into our conduct with everyone, especially by submitting to the authorities in a spirit of obedience without murmuring. The author sees that God, the Ruler of all, has permitted the existence of those in authority, even if they are unjust, so in wisdom we submit to them in the Lord. This submission rests on two principles: our faith in God's surpassing providence for us, and our enjoyment of a quiet and peaceful life.

8.1.2.en: a. "I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God" [2].

8.1.3.en: Here is a call to submit to the laws and be committed to respecting them, but the limit of this obedience is "the oath (the vow) of the Lord," that is, without violating our obligations toward God or our covenant with Him, for it is above every obligation. As the Lord Christ says: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

8.1.4.en: In the same spirit St. Paul says: "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation" (Rom 3:1-2).

8.2.0.en: b. We must not rebel against him, resist him or refuse his service because his actions are not accepted by our reason or wrong us. In wisdom we must not hasten to leave him and go out from before him, for the sake of our peace, avoiding his anger and fury. Let us wait, for God does not leave injustice to prevail but intervenes at the proper time. The Preacher says: "Be not hasty to go out of his sight" [3]. The people were hasty when Rehoboam the son of Solomon answered them roughly and harshly, and they hastened to go from his presence, indeed they cried out at once: "To your tents, O Israel" (1 Kgs 12:16), and the kingdom was divided for long centuries!

8.2.1.en: c. We must not persist in error when we discover it: "Stand not in an evil thing; for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him" [3]. When we think wrongly against one who holds authority, we must turn back and not go on in the error.

8.2.2.en: d. As long as we keep the commandment and walk in a spirit of obedience and wisdom, we do not fear the power that the word of those in authority holds...

8.2.3.en: "Where the word of a king is, there is power:

8.2.4.en: and who may say unto him, What doest thou?

8.3.0.en: Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment" [4-5].

8.3.1.en: The Preacher does not deny the capacity of the one who holds authority, for he cannot bear to see anyone disobey his word, and as the wise man says: "The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion" (Prov 19:12)... There is none who says to him: What doest thou? Yet there is no danger in this, as long as our hearts are pure, keep the laws and obey them gladly, and our minds are full of wisdom, knowing how to act at the proper time.

8.4.0.en: 6 Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him. 7 For he knoweth not that which shall be: for who can tell him when it shall be? 8 There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it.

8.4.1.en: As long as we keep the Lord's commandment and accept the word of rulers in the Lord, we must not fear authority, nor be troubled by what may befall us tomorrow, nor even by facing death; we fear one thing only, which is to sin, for "wickedness [shall not] deliver those that are given to it."

8.4.2.en: a. "Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man is great upon him."

8.4.3.en: It befits the wise man to understand that for everything there is a suitable time with God; nothing happens by chance, but by the wisdom of God, the Ruler of all. Everything is reckoned with God, and its time is appointed by a divine plan or by divine permission, but man, in his ignorance of God's plan and judgments and his lack of full trust in His surpassing providence, falls into great evil.

8.4.4.en: Man needs the enlightenment of his inner sight by the Spirit of God, so that he does not think that a certain event befalls him without purpose... but rather leans on the breast of his Creator, thanks Him for joyful events, and benefits from His chastenings, knowing that all things work together for good to those who love Him (Rom 8:28). Joseph could not have received glory in Pharaoh's palace had he not first been trained in the school of life, understanding that his brethren had done him evil, but with divine permission, who turned their evil into good (Gen 50:20).

8.4.5.en: Our great evil comes upon us not because of the circumstances that surround us, however harsh they may seem, but because of the veil over our inner sight. The work of the Holy Spirit is to give us enlightenment, so that we perceive that we are children of God, the object of His love, who cares even for the number of the hairs of our heads, who holds our hands amid events on the narrow way of the Cross so as to bring us into the breadth and joy of the Resurrection.

8.4.6.en: b. "For he knoweth not that which shall be: for who can tell him when it shall be?

8.5.0.en: There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it" [7-8].

8.6.0.en: All of us are ignorant of the future, its events, circumstances and times, and no one can tell us what will befall us so that we may prepare for emergencies. We do not know the evil before it happens so that we may avoid it or guard against it... but we know one thing by which we face the future with all its events and surprises: "neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it" [8].

8.6.2.en: * An unknown future, with events that may seem sudden and unexpected.

8.6.3.en: * Inability to retain our spirits when they are demanded, that is, we cannot postpone the hour of our departure from this world, where the door of repentance is closed forever.

8.6.4.en: * We cannot be discharged from the war [8], that is, from entering the battle that is raging between God and the devil, whether we enter under God's protection or accept submission to the enemy of good.

8.6.5.en: These three things are turned to our good if we entrust ourselves to the righteousness of Christ, the Giver of peace, victory and glory; if we think that we cannot live in an evil world unless we walk with cunning, craftiness and evil as a human wisdom and an experience we acquire over time, then evil will not deliver us here on earth, nor in our meeting with the just Judge on the great day of the Lord.

8.7.0.en: 9 All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every work that is done under the sun: there is a time wherein one man ruleth over another to his own hurt. 10 And so I saw the wicked buried, who had come and gone from the place of the holy, and they were forgotten in the city where they had so done: this is also vanity.

8.7.1.en: Perhaps someone asks: How can I obey those in authority if they are unjust and lovers of domination? The Preacher says:

8.7.2.en: "All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every work that is done under the sun: there is a time wherein one man ruleth over another to his own hurt" [9].

8.7.3.en: Truly it is hard for a man to see a person who is a tyrant, a lover of domination and of oppressing others, and it is grievous to see some leaders on the religious or worldly level, instead of establishing justice, exploiting their positions for their own glory or wealth; but let these know that by this they practice what is to their own hurt.

8.7.4.en: When we see tyrants we do not condemn them but pity them and pray for them, that God may grant them a spirit of self-giving love and humility, so that they neither cause anyone to stumble nor perish themselves.

8.8.0.en: Furthermore, it befits the unjust to understand that even if they obtain something by their injustice, whether wealth or honor, they will be buried and their memory forgotten. The Preacher says: "And so I saw the wicked buried" [10], that is, their bodies are cast into the dust and their honor with them. The Preacher continues his discourse about them, saying: "And they were gathered, those who come and go from the place of the holy and receive honor, and they were forgotten in the city. This is also vanity" (10 N IV and Vulgate). Truly, as leaders who enter the sanctuaries and go out from them in grandeur, and the place of judgment was called "holy" in the Old Testament because "the judgment is God's" (Deut 1:17), as it is said that God "judgeth among the gods" (Ps 82:1), etc... Under the cover of this grandeur they commit injustice and persist in it, but their bodies become dust and their memory is buried with them... The holy city forgets them, and they have no place in the heavenly Jerusalem, into which nothing defiled or unclean enters, nor whoever works falsehood and injustice.

8.8.1.en: In their recklessness they hasten unjust judgment, and God in His longsuffering bears with them and leaves them in their positions for a time, that perhaps they may repent; otherwise their memory is buried with their bodies, and they lose both temporal and eternal things.

8.9.s.en: 5. Wisdom and the prosperity of the wicked:

8.9.0.en: 11 Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. 12 Though a sinner do evil an hundred times, and his days be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him: 13 But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he prolong his days, which are as a shadow; because he feareth not before God. 14 There is a vanity which is done upon the earth; that there be just men, unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked; again, there be wicked men, to whom it happeneth according to the work of the righteous: I said that this also is vanity.

8.9.1.en: God is patient with the unjust, and indeed with all the wicked, and the judgment is not executed speedily... But many, instead of repenting, make light of God's longsuffering. As the Apostle Paul says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:4-6). This is what the Preacher expressed, saying:

8.9.2.en: "Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil" [11].

8.9.3.en: God delays a little in punishment, but it will surely come to pass, and sternly, especially since some misunderstand God's longsuffering and fill up the cup of their evil.

8.9.4.en: Perhaps someone asks: And what of the fault of the oppressed?

8.9.5.en: The Preacher answers: Even if evil increases, it is turned into good for those who fear the Lord.

8.9.6.en: "Though a sinner do evil an hundred times, and his days be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him:

8.10.0.en: But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he prolong his days, which are as a shadow; because he feareth not before God" [12-13].

8.10.1.en: Some may object, saying that God's longsuffering has reached a limit beyond what we expect, and the days of the wicked man have been prolonged so that he commits evil not once or twice or ten times but a hundred times; but let these know that the people of God, or those who truly fear Him, even if oppression falls upon them hundreds of times, are a blessed people. They fear the Lord, therefore He accompanies them in the darkest circumstances; nothing can shake their happiness, nor can anything cut off their fellowship with God; even in the midst of their troubles they are filled with inner peace, because they are kept by God their Father, who rescues them from affliction and glorifies them.

8.10.2.en: The wicked, on the contrary, though they seem fresh like grass, are in their depths filled with misery; good finds no place in them, and blessedness does not know them. They may live in luxury for a period of time, but the curse, as the natural fruit of their deeds, surely comes upon them unless they repent and return to God in fear and trembling. As it is said: "Say ye to the righteous, that it shall be well with him: for they shall eat the fruit of their doings. Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him" (Isa 3:10-11).

8.10.3.en: However long the days of the wicked man may be, they are like a shadow, ending without profit. We may think they are long, but in God's eyes they are like a swiftly passing shadow.

8.11.0.en: The thermometer by which the wise man recognizes the righteous and the wicked and distinguishes between them is "the fear of God," so he calls the righteous "them that fear God," and says of the wicked that they "feareth not before God." As for outward appearance, temporal blessings or death, the righteous may fall into afflictions and troubles that the wicked deserve, and the wicked may enjoy temporal blessings that the righteous deserve. This is what reveals the vanity of the world [14], without accusing God of injustice, for He waits to reward all and repay them at the proper time.

8.12.s.en: 6. Reflection on God's work and gifts:

8.12.0.en: 15 Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be merry: for that shall abide with him of his labour the days of his life, which God giveth him under the sun. 16 When I applied mine heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth: (for also there is that neither day nor night seeth sleep with his eyes:) 17 Then I beheld all the work of God, that a man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun: because though a man labour to seek it out, yet he shall not find it; yea further; though a wise man think to know it, yet shall he not be able to find it.

8.12.1.en: The injustice that befalls the world reveals the vanity of the world, but it does not make the believer lose his inner joy; rather he gives thanks to God under all circumstances, counting his eating, drinking and labor as God's temporary gift [15]. This is what the wise man repeats in more than one place (Eccl 2:24; 5:18).

8.12.2.en: The wise man stresses the believer's enjoyment of joy as the food of the soul: "I commended mirth," counting it a divine gift... The secret of his joy is his contemplation of God's work on earth and his contact with His wonders, which took sleep from his eyes, so that he remains rejoicing day and night in God who works in his life and in the lives of others... even though his personal wisdom prevents him from knowing all the secrets of God's dealings with him and His surpassing care for His children.

8.13.0.en: He says: "When I applied mine heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth: for also there is that neither day nor night seeth sleep with his eyes" [16].

8.14.0.en: The wise man himself meant that in his inquiry into God's providence he did not see sleep... but, as he says: "Though a wise man think to know it, yet shall he not be able to find it" [17]... His wisdom is unable to find or discover God's plan and His wonderful purposes, which surpass the mind!

8.14.1.en: Let us walk in divine wisdom, so that the eyes of our hearts may be enlightened and His grace may shine on our features, and with joy let us walk in a spirit of obedience and submission, and if injustice is found, let us believe in God our Father, who redeems our life from the pit and turns troubles to our good. He is patient with the wicked that perhaps they may return to Him, otherwise their lives become like a worthless shadow... How wonderful is Your work, O Lord! Grant me understanding and enlightenment, that I may perceive by Your Holy Spirit Your plan for me!
